nghe.t: Part 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman who wants to join a kayaking club and the club secretary. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 10.
Good morning, Riverside Paddle Club, Mark speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hello. I saw your poster in the library, and I'd like to join the club, if that's possible.
Of course. I can take your details now and you can start next week. Could I have your name, please?
Yes, it's Sophie Farrant. That's F, A, double R, A, N, T.
F, A, R, R, A, N, T. Thank you. And your address?
I live at 18 Harbour Road. Harbour is spelt the British way, with O, U, R.
Harbour Road, got it. And a contact number?
My mobile is 07945 812 663.
So that's 07945 812 663. Lovely. Now, have you done any kayaking before?
A little. I've never had proper lessons, but I tried it a few times on holiday in Croatia last summer.
That's a good start. We'll put you in the improvers' group, then. Which session would suit you best? We run beginners and improvers on Wednesday and Thursday evenings.
Wednesday would be ideal… oh, actually, no — I've just remembered I have a seminar on Wednesday evenings this term. Thursday, please.
Thursday it is. Now, there are different types of membership. A standard adult membership is sixty pounds a term.
Is there a discount for students? I'm at the university.
Yes, there is. If you show your student card at your first session, the student membership is forty-five pounds a term instead of sixty.
Great, I'll take the student membership, then. Do I need to bring anything? A wetsuit?
No, we provide wetsuits, helmets and buoyancy aids. You just need to bring a change of clothes and a towel, because you will almost certainly get wet.
Right. And where should I go on the first evening? Is it at the boathouse?
The boathouse is being repaired at the moment, so for the next few weeks we're meeting by the old footbridge, just past the car park. You can't miss it.
The footbridge. OK. Oh, and should I mention any health conditions?
Yes, please. It helps our instructors.
I have mild asthma. It doesn't usually cause problems, but I always carry an inhaler.
Thanks, I'll make a note of the asthma. Bring the inhaler in a waterproof bag and give it to the instructor before you go on the water. We look forward to seeing you on Thursday.

nghe.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a newly renovated market hall. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Kingsford Market Hall. My name's James, and I'll be showing you around today.

Let me start with a little history. Because of the great iron and glass roof, a lot of visitors assume that this building was once a railway station. In fact, it was built in the 1880s as a wool exchange, where farmers and merchants met to agree prices. It only became a fish market much later, in the 1930s, and it closed altogether about twenty years ago.

When the council decided to renovate the hall, there was a lot of discussion about what it should be used for. Some people wanted a museum to attract tourists. But in the end the main aim was to give small local businesses an affordable place to trade, and that's why most of the stalls are rented by independent makers and food producers from the area. Restoring the roof was certainly expensive, but it was part of the job rather than the reason for it.

A quick word about opening times. The hall is open every day from eight in the morning, and that hasn't changed. What is new is that on Fridays we now stay open until ten at night, with live music in the evenings.

One piece of advice: our guided tours of the roof walkway are very popular and limited to twelve people, so I'd strongly recommend booking them online before you come. Almost all stalls take cards these days, so there's no need to bring cash, and the car park is usually full by ten, so the bus is a better option.
Now, if you look at the plan of the ground floor, I'll show you where everything is. We're standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan.
Directly in front of you, before you reach the fountain, you'll see the information desk. That's the place to go if you need a map or you've lost something.
The small room immediately on your left as you come in is the ticket office for the roof tours. And just to the right of the entrance is the gift shop, which sells work by local artists.
If you walk straight past the fountain to the back wall, the café is right there in the middle, facing the entrance. It has the best view of the roof.
Parents, please note that the children's play area is halfway along the left-hand wall, opposite the flower stalls, which are on the right-hand side.
The exhibition room, which tells the story of the wool trade, is in the far left-hand corner, at the back of the hall.
And finally, the toilets. They're at the back on the right, next to the stairs that lead up to the roof walkway — so not in the corner itself, but just beside the stairs.
Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start with the exhibition room.

nghe.t: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Tom, talking to their tutor about their project on urban heat. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 30.
Come in, Maya, Tom. So, how is the urban heat project going?
Pretty well, mostly. We put twenty temperature sensors around the city centre and the park for two weeks.
Although it wasn't all smooth. We were really worried that some of the sensors would be stolen, but actually none of them were.
The bigger issue was that the cheap sensors we bought didn't always agree with each other. Two sensors placed side by side could be almost a degree apart.
And we couldn't get permission to fix sensors on two of the office buildings we wanted, so there's a gap in the business district.
Those are both common problems. Did the weather cooperate?
It was a normal September, really — nothing unusual. And we finished on schedule.

Good. Now, you're presenting this to the class in three weeks. I've read your draft. My main comment is that the literature review takes up almost half of your talk. You need to cut that down considerably so there's more time for your own results.
That makes sense. We could also include the interviews we did with shop owners.

I'd leave those out, to be honest — there were only four, and they distract from the data. What would really help is a map of the city showing where each sensor was and the temperatures it recorded. People understand heat islands much faster when they can see them.
OK, a map. We'll do that. Should we use more slides, then?
No — fewer, clearer slides are better. Now, what about your sources?
Well, there's the city council report on green spaces. It's very relevant, but the temperature figures are from 2015, so we need to find out whether there's a newer version before we use it.
Yes, definitely check that first.
Then there's a newspaper article that claims the city centre is ten degrees hotter than the countryside. It's quite dramatic, but there's no explanation of how they measured it.
If you can't tell how the figure was produced, it doesn't belong in an academic project.
Agreed, we'll drop it. And the satellite images from the space agency are excellent — they match our own readings really well, so they're definitely going in.
Good. So what are your next steps?
First, we'll borrow a standard thermometer from the physics lab and compare each sensor against it, so we can correct the readings.
Then we want to repeat the measurements, but this time at night, because that's when the difference between the centre and the park should be biggest.
Very sensible. And after that?
We'd like to share what we found with local residents. The community centre has offered us a room for a workshop next month.
Excellent. A workshop is a great way to get feedback. Well done, both of you.

nghe.t: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about the sounds made by coral reefs. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Good morning. Today I want to talk about something most people never think of when they imagine a coral reef: its sound.

If you have ever put your head underwater on a healthy reef, you will know that it is anything but silent. The background noise is a constant crackle, rather like fat sizzling in a frying pan. Most of that crackle comes from snapping shrimp, tiny animals that close a special claw so fast that it creates a bubble, and the bubble collapses with a loud snap.
On top of that, the fish themselves are surprisingly vocal. Different species grunt, croak and even produce whistles, especially at dawn and dusk.

Why does this matter? Well, most reef fish spend the first weeks of their lives as larvae drifting in the open ocean. When they are ready, they have to find a reef to live on, and there is good evidence that they listen for the sound of a healthy reef when they choose where to settle.

The problem is that damaged reefs sound very different. When coral dies, the animals that depend on it disappear, and a degraded reef becomes much quieter. That means it attracts fewer young fish, which in turn makes recovery even slower.

A team working on the Great Barrier Reef in Australia decided to test whether sound could break this cycle. They took recordings from healthy parts of the reef. Then they placed underwater speakers on patches of reef that had been badly damaged, and played the recordings back every night for several weeks.

The results were striking. Compared with similar patches where no sound was played, the number of young fish arriving roughly doubled. And it was not just more of the same fish — there were also more species, which matters, because different fish do different jobs, such as grazing on the seaweed that can smother coral.

However, I want to be clear about the limitations. Playing sound cannot, on its own, bring back the coral. If the water stays too warm, or pollution continues, the reef will not recover however many fish arrive.
There is also a risk. If we attract young fish to an area that offers them no food or shelter, we may be leading them into a trap, where they are easily eaten by predators.

So the next step for researchers is long-term monitoring, to find out whether the fish that arrive actually survive and help the reef to recover over several years. Only then will we know whether this technique deserves a place in reef conservation.

READING PASSAGE 1
GUARDIANS OF THE COAST
How mangrove forests survive where other trees cannot — and why they matter

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow in the intertidal zone of tropical and subtropical coastlines — the strip of muddy shore that is flooded by the sea twice a day and exposed again when the tide goes out. Around seventy species are recognised, and together they cover roughly 150,000 square kilometres, an area about half the size of Vietnam. Few woody plants can tolerate such conditions. The water that washes around their trunks contains a high level of salt, the soil is soft and unstable, and every few hours the roots are either drowned or left baking in the sun.
Salt is the first problem. Most plants die quickly if their roots sit in seawater, because salt draws water out of their cells. Mangroves deal with it in several ways. Some species filter out more than ninety per cent of the salt at the surface of their roots, so that the water reaching the rest of the tree is almost fresh. Others allow salt into their tissues but then get rid of it through special glands in their leaves; on a dry afternoon, a careful observer can see tiny white crystals glittering on the leaf surface. Interestingly, mangroves do not actually need salt. nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 2
THE BOX THAT CHANGED THE WORLD
The humble shipping container transformed trade — and created problems of its own

A  For most of history, loading a ship was slow, expensive and dangerous work. Cargo travelled as "break-bulk": sacks of coffee, barrels of oil, crates of machinery and bundles of timber, each lifted on and off by teams of dockworkers. A single cargo ship might carry tens of thousands of separate items, and a large vessel could spend a week or more in port being unloaded and reloaded — in some cases nearly as long as it spent at sea. Theft was common, goods were frequently damaged, and the cost of handling cargo at the two ends of a journey often exceeded the cost of the voyage itself.
B  The idea that eventually swept this system away came not from a shipping company but from a road haulier. Malcom McLean, who had built up a large trucking business in the United States, grew frustrated watching his drivers wait for hours while their loads were transferred to ships. His solution was simple: rather than unloading the goods, why not lift the whole trailer box onto the vessel? In 1956 a converted tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight such boxes. According to most accounts, the cost of loading fell by more than ninety per cent compared with traditional methods.
C  Yet a box on its own changed very little. Early containers came in many shapes and sizes, and each shipping line used its own design, which meant that a box from one company could not be carried by another company's ships or lifted by its cranes. The real breakthrough came in the late 1960s, when international committees agreed on a small number of standard dimensions, together with standard corner fittings that allowed any crane, truck or train wagon to lock onto any box. Capacity is still measured today in "twenty-foot equivalent units", or TEU, a direct legacy of those negotiations. The maritime historian Daniel Okafor argues that "the container's success depended on committees as much as on engineers; without agreement on size, it would have remained a clever local trick."
D  For the people who worked on the docks, the consequences were severe. A ship that once required hundreds of workers for a week could now be emptied by a few crane operators in a day. In port cities on both sides of the Atlantic, dock employment collapsed within a generation, and neighbourhoods that had depended on waterfront jobs for a century fell into decline. "The machines arrived faster than any community could retrain," says Priya Raman, who studies labour history. "Whole districts lost not only their income but their sense of purpose."
E  Elsewhere, the effects were far more positive. As the cost of moving goods fell, it became practical for companies to make different parts of a product in different countries and assemble them somewhere else again. The logistics engineer Hiroshi Tanabe points out that containers allowed factories to keep very small stocks of components, because parts could be scheduled to arrive exactly when they were needed. The port economist Marta Lindqvist goes further, suggesting that cheaper freight was not the most important change at all. "What manufacturers really valued," she says, "was predictability. A container that arrives on the day it was promised is worth more than one that is cheap but late."
F  Seventy years on, the container system faces new pressures. Ships have grown enormously — the largest now carry more than twenty thousand boxes — and only a handful of harbours in the world have water deep enough and cranes tall enough to serve them. Because global supply chains are so tightly linked, a problem in one place can spread rapidly. When a single giant vessel ran aground in the Suez Canal in March 2021, blocking it for six days, the knock-on hold-ups were felt by shipping companies and manufacturers across the globe for months afterwards. The box that made the world smaller has also made it more fragile.

READING PASSAGE 2
THE BOX THAT CHANGED THE WORLD
The humble shipping container transformed trade — and created problems of its own

A  For most of history, loading a ship was slow, expensive and dangerous work. Cargo travelled as "break-bulk": sacks of coffee, barrels of oil, crates of machinery and bundles of timber, each lifted on and off by teams of dockworkers. A single cargo ship might carry tens of thousands of separate items, and a large vessel could spend a week or more in port being unloaded and reloaded — in some cases nearly as long as it spent at sea. Theft was common, goods were frequently damaged, and the cost of handling cargo at the two ends of a journey often exceeded the cost of the voyage itself.
B  The idea that eventually swept this system away came not from a shipping company but from a road haulier. Malcom McLean, who had built up a large trucking business in the United States, grew frustrated watching his drivers wait for hours while their loads were transferred to ships. His solution was simple: rather than unloading the goods, why not lift the whole trailer box onto the vessel? In 1956 a converted tanker called the Ideal X sailed from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight such boxes. According to most accounts, the cost of loading fell by more than ninety per cent compared with traditional methods.
C  Yet a box on its own changed very little. Early containers came in many shapes and sizes, and each shipping line used its own design, which meant that a box from one company could not be carried by another company's ships or lifted by its cranes. The real breakthrough came in the late 1960s, when international committees agreed on a small number of standard dimensions, together with standard corner fittings that allowed any crane, truck or train wagon to lock onto any box. Capacity is still measured today in "twenty-foot equivalent units", or TEU, a direct legacy of those negotiations. The maritime historian Daniel Okafor argues that "the container's success depended on committees as much as on engineers; without agreement on size, it would have remained a clever local trick."
D  For the people who worked on the docks, the consequences were severe. A ship that once required hundreds of workers for a week could now be emptied by a few crane operators in a day. In port cities on both sides of the Atlantic, dock employment collapsed within a generation, and neighbourhoods that had depended on waterfront jobs for a century fell into decline. "The machines arrived faster than any community could retrain," says Priya Raman, who studies labour history. "Whole districts lost not only their income but their sense of purpose."
E  Elsewhere, the effects were far more positive. As the cost of moving goods fell, it became practical for companies to make different parts of a product in different countries and assemble them somewhere else again. The logistics engineer Hiroshi Tanabe points out that containers allowed factories to keep very small stocks of components, because parts could be scheduled to arrive exactly when they were needed. The port economist Marta Lindqvist goes further, suggesting that cheaper freight was not the most important change at all. "What manufacturers really valued," she says, "was predictability. A container that arrives on the day it was promised is worth more than one that is cheap but late."
F  Seventy years on, the container system faces new pressures. Ships have grown enormously — the largest now carry more than twenty thousand boxes — and only a handful of harbours in the world have water deep enough and cranes tall enough to serve them. Because global supply chains are so tightly linked, a problem in one place can spread rapidly. When a single giant vessel ran aground in the Suez Canal in March 2021, blocking it for six days, the knock-on hold-ups were felt by shipping companies and manufacturers across the globe for months afterwards. The box that made the world smaller has also made it more fragile.

nhom.doan:
READING PASSAGE 3
THE HIDDEN VALUE OF BOREDOM
Is the feeling we try hardest to avoid actually good for us?

Few experiences are as universally disliked as boredom. For centuries it has been treated as a minor moral failing — the problem of idle people who lacked the discipline to find something useful to do. Psychologists, for their part, largely ignored it, regarding it as too vague and too ordinary to deserve serious study. Over the past two decades, however, that attitude has changed, and researchers now see boredom as a distinct emotion with its own causes, consequences and, surprisingly, its own benefits. In my view, this shift is overdue: boredom is a far more useful feeling than its reputation suggests.
Most researchers now agree that boredom is best understood as a signal. Just as hunger tells us that we need food, boredom tells us that what we are doing — or not doing — has stopped engaging our minds. It is uncomfortable precisely so that we will act on it. Like physical pain, its unpleasantness is the point: a signal that could easily be ignored would be of little use. Seen this way, boredom is not the opposite of motivation but one of its sources, pushing us to change our situation and look for something more meaningful.
Some evidence suggests that boredom may even make us more creative. In one well-known British experiment, volunteers were first asked to copy telephone numbers from a directory for fifteen minutes, a task chosen because it was almost perfectly dull. They were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with a group who had gone straight to the creative task, the bored volunteers came up with more ideas. The researchers suggested that the dull task had encouraged mind-wandering, allowing the volunteers' thoughts to drift and make unexpected connections. The effect was modest, and not every later study has confirmed it, but it fits with the reports of many writers and scientists who say their best ideas arrive when they are doing nothing in particular.
Not all boredom is harmless, though. Psychologists distinguish between situational boredom, which arises from a particular dull task and disappears when the task ends, and chronic boredom, a lasting tendency to find life unstimulating. It is the second kind that worries researchers. People who are easily bored are more likely to engage in risky behaviour such as gambling, and they report higher levels of anxiety and low mood. Whether boredom causes these problems or simply accompanies them is still debated, but the link is consistent enough to take seriously.
Many of us, it seems, will go to great lengths to avoid even a few minutes of boredom. In a series of studies in the United States, participants were left alone in a plain room for up to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. In one version, they could press a button to give themselves a mild electric shock — one that most had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. A quarter of the women and two-thirds of the men chose to shock themselves at least once. The finding says less about pain than about how uncomfortable many of us are when left alone with our own thoughts.
Today, of course, we rarely need to be. A smartphone offers an instant escape from any empty moment: a queue, a bus journey, the thirty seconds while a kettle boils. An entire industry of games, feeds and short videos has grown up around that need. Yet phones do not cure boredom; they merely postpone it, and the constant switching from one small distraction to the next often leaves people feeling flatter and more restless than before. We cannot know for certain whether we are more bored than our grandparents were, because nobody measured boredom in the past. What has clearly changed is how rarely we allow the feeling to run its course.
What, then, should we do? It would be a mistake to try to remove every dull moment from children's lessons; learning to stay with a difficult or repetitive task is itself a skill that school should teach. For adults, the most practical advice is to treat boredom as information rather than as an emergency. When it appears, it is worth asking what it is telling us — that a task needs a new approach, perhaps, or that we need a break of a different kind. Some people find it helpful to set aside regular periods without screens, such as a walk with no headphones, so that the mind has space to wander. None of this will make boredom pleasant. But it may allow us to hear what it has been trying to say.
